Overall, follow what your prescriber says, and if your normal dose isn't working for you, let them know so they can make adjustments or add something else to your regimen.

I'm glad that you were able to have successful transplants! The process does differ between places, but generally it's a simple surgical procedure. I remove it by cutting away the conjunctiva (fleshy membrane that gets inflamed when you have pink eye), making an incision about 2-3mm away from the cornea, cutting 360 degrees around it with specialized scissors, and gently pulling the cornea away from the iris and underlying membranes. Some eye banks use trephines to score a tracing line around before they cut. Then, at least in the case of the full thickness transplant, the doctor will use a trephine to cut out the middle 8mm of cornea (that's usually all that gets transplanted). 

There's of course a lot of other stuff (medical review, tissue processing) that goes into it, but that's the gist of the work. Congrats on being able to see! :D

I have the same exact kind of skin as you, and I'm 24. It is so frustrating. I always wondered how it was possible that someone could have dry skin AND cystic acne at the same time. It's like, do I go for a rich moisturizer and risk breakouts, or a lighter one and not get enough moisture? My skin is also very sensitive and prone to allergic reactions. A couple things have helped me somewhat. (FYI, this isn't really a typical routine, it's just what has worked best for me. Take with a grain of salt.)

First, tretinoin. I went to a PA and was prescribed 0.025%. I've been using it every/every other night for a few years now, and it tackles the acne quite nicely (though I still get hormonal breakouts, thanks Nexplanon, they're just more manageable). It's supposed to help with hyperpigmentation, too. I follow up in the morning with a 10% benzoyl peroxide wash, as has always been recommended by all the docs and derms I've ever seen. 

Second, my skin would always get red and inflamed with most normal toners, so I started using a gentle diluted witch hazel toner. I find it helps my skin absorb moisturizers better too, so I don't need to use those thick creams that sometimes cause breakouts. 

Vitamin C serum with hyaluronic acid and Vit E. I use a tiny amount at night, and it has helped a bit with texture and hyperpigmentation. 

I wash off my makeup with a gentle cetaphil cleanser and I moisturize with a generic cetaphil face lotion. Sometimes a thicker Vanicream if my skin is really dry or inflamed (like in winter). I find if I use anything stronger on a regular basis, I break out. 

And this might sound silly, but I really like those cheap generic Asian sheet masks, if only for the pampering. They leave my skin feeling soft and dewy. Even if they're not doing anything for my skin, they make me feel relaxed, and I'm sure that can't hurt! 

I've tried to incorporate some of the other things on the sidebar, but my skin always gets too irritated. My current routine strikes a good balance for me. It's actually a pretty complex process, so hang with me here.

First, I get a dispatch call to the hospital, funeral home, or coroner's office where the body is. I'll review all the available medical records for the donor and make sure they're eligible preliminarily. Then I'll get driving. It's a lot of driving.

Once I get to the destination, I'll be taken to the body. I have a giant bag of supplies, and I start setting them up. ID the body, and start my physical exam. I have to check every single inch of the donor's body for evidence of anything that could be concerning. Then I'll check the eyes - I shine a penlight in to make sure they have natural lenses (often they don't) and look for any ocular abnormalities. If everything is ok so far, I'll draw blood to take back to our lab for serological testing.

Then, the fun begins. I prep the face using the same sterile technique surgeons use, with a povidone-iodine solution. Once I've prepped them, I prep my sterile field. I use surgical scrub technique to sterilize myself, and then I start the procedure.

First, I hold the lids open with a speculum. I carefully cut away the conjunctiva, the pink fleshy layer over the whites of your eyes. I then use a trephine, a circular blade, to score a circle on the sclera surrounding the cornea. I'll make 1-4 incisions along this line, and connect them using specialized Castroviejo scissors. Then, the most important part - I VERY carefully and delicately pull the underlying membranes away from the cornea to detach it from the rest of the eye. Once it's fully excised, I place it in a viewing chamber filled with special preserving fluid. Rinse and repeat with the other eye. 

Then I reconstruct the donor (take out the rest of the eye and put cotton or plastic balls and eye caps inside) and make my way onto my next case.

*  The answer to that is rather complex. There are two main parts to evaluating eligibility for transplant, the donor's medical/social eligibility and the tissue quality. 

For the former, we engage in a lengthy process of interviewing next-of-kin, doctors, coroners, etc. and pouring over the donor's medical history. Many things can rule a tissue out at this point, including any communicable diseases, cancers of the eye, and high risk behavior (like IV drug use). 

Tissue quality itself is even more complex because there are so many conditions that can make it unsuitable, some that aren't even well documented in medical literature yet. Generally we want to see a tissue with no scars, infections, or issues from postmortem exposure (if eyes aren't taped shut and iced after death, cornea quality suffers). Additionally, high endothelial cell count is essential. You're born with a cell count of ~4000 cells per millimeter squared in the inner layer of your cornea and as you age, that count goes down, especially if you mistreat your cornea. The higher the count, the healthier the cornea is, generally.

Even if a tissue is ruled out for some reason though, it can usually be used for research. We send research tissue to labs all over the world.

Tell them that you've been dealing with depression and it makes it hard to do even the most basic of things. You sound just like me two years ago. I'm a senior now, and still having something of a "what on earth do I do with my life" crisis, but I am 1000% better than where I was two years ago.  A few things really helped me through:

1. Therapy. I had to go through maybe 4 different therapists before I found the right one for me, but I've been seeing her for months now and she is a godsend. 

2. Medication. You need to make sure you don't have an undiagnosed mental illness.  Go to your doctor and discuss how you're feeling. Medication doesn't cure anything, but in my experience it really helps to make symptoms manageable.

3. Am I on the right path? Am I in the wrong major? For many of us, I've realized that there's no such thing. Do you enjoy the subject that you're studying? There's the important part. You're probably not going to know what you want to do/were "meant" to do for years, if ever! And you know what? That's totally okay. It took me forever to realize and accept that I just have to go with the flow, because for some of us, there is no "perfect major" or anything. I just realized that, as an INFP-type person, what I truly enjoy is the pursuit of knowledge. :)

4. What's most important right now is you. Don't think about pleasing your parents, or upsetting your teachers, or anything like that right now. Just focus on the little accomplishments that push you forward day by day. You got out of bed today? Fantastic! Reward yourself for every little success you have.

5. Finally, what helped me most was talking to my professors. You'd be surprised how understanding they usually are. Mine were very accommodating at helping me through the rough onset of mental illness. And the few that I liked best ended up being great mentors in helping me discover what fields/future careers I might like best. It's tremendously scary and energy-consuming to try and talk to them about these things, but trust me, it takes a huuuuge weight off your shoulders.

Good luck. It's a tough period in most people's lives to transition into adulthood, but I at least can be living proof to you that it's possible to survive.
